episode_title: What The Dashboard Can't Tell You

real_qa.q: What practices can project managers use to identify team members who are on track but running on empty?
real_qa.r: Ask a consistent question in regular check-ins such as 'How are things really going beyond what the status shows?' This question doesn't ask anyone to confess or label them, but leaves room for the part of the story that processes and tools can't hold. Keep the question the same each time so it becomes part of the rhythm. When someone responds that they stretched, say thank you and ask what would help most right now, which may be something you can carry to the sponsor or simply knowing that you know.
real_qa.requete: How to identify team members running on empty in project management

real_qa.q: What does the March 2026 Harvard Business Review study reveal about AI tool overuse and team productivity?
real_qa.r: A March 2026 Harvard Business Review study of nearly 1,500 full-time U.S. workers found that 14% reported what researchers call AI brain fry—mental fatigue from excessive use or oversight of AI tools beyond a person's cognitive capacity. People experiencing this described brain fog, trouble focusing, slower decision making, and more errors. Productivity increased when moving from one AI tool to two, rose by less with a third, and dipped after that. Teams with fewer signs of brain fry had leaders available to discuss AI concerns, clear AI training, and AI built into existing workflows.
real_qa.requete: Harvard Business Review March 2026 AI brain fry study results

real_qa.q: How should project managers handle a risk concern shared confidentially by a team member?
real_qa.r: Listen first and fix nothing yet, then ask what the team member needs from you—whether they want it raised or simply want you to know. If it goes into the risk log, record the risk itself rather than the person, documenting what the concern is, what it could affect, and next steps, with attribution only if they agree. Know where it goes next, whether that's a sponsor, manager, HR, or an employee assistance program, and follow up to show that what was shared was taken seriously.
real_qa.requete: How to handle confidential risk concerns from team members as a project manager

real_qa.q: What is the recommended frequency and format for peer check-ins among project managers?
real_qa.r: Set a short standing check-in every couple of weeks with a peer or another PM in a similar role. In these meetings, discuss what's weighing on you, what's working, and what you need—with no names shared, competencies kept private, and no fixing unless asked for. Trade practices like the questions covered, and turn the standing question inward: 'What is the data not telling me about how I'm actually doing?' This peer support works alongside professional care and is a good source of support for the isolation that project professionals often experience.
real_qa.requete: Peer check-in frequency and format for project managers

real_qa.q: Why is honoring mental health essential to keeping a project plan connected to reality?
real_qa.r: Being seen and heard is what makes a team honest. Acknowledging concerns, making sure every stakeholder gets to speak, and being adaptable to what the team needs doesn't compete with the plan—it keeps the plan connected to reality. A conversation takes time and may not fit neatly into a status report, but giving it a small, regular place is enough. Mental health support is not a soft add-on to project delivery; it's what enables team members to speak up while there's still time to act on issues.
real_qa.requete: Mental health project management team honesty reality
